newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian parliament endorses clearing of Di Rupo.
newsitem.headline: Belgian parliament endorses clearing of Di Rupo.

text.p: Belgium's parliament on Thursday endorsed a parliamentary commission's finding that cleared Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo of allegations he had sex with under-age boys.
The full legislature adopted the advice of the commission, in which the main parties were present, by a vote of 79 to 62.

Commission chairman Raymond Langendries had earlier told reporters: "The commission...considers that, in the present state of the reports sent to parliament (by the public prosecutor), there are no indications of guilt and therefore no elements that would justify his (Di Rupo's) indictment."
Prior to sending it to the full house, the commission had accepted by a vote of seven to four the finding, which emerged early on Thursday morning after three days and nights of often bitter debate.

But the commission's split vote showed the strains within the centre-left coalition over the decision, with Di Rupo's fellow socialists backing him and the Christian Democrat partners principally seeking to limit any political damage.
The result triggered opposition charges of a cover-up.
"This is an exclusively political decision," said Didier Reynders, a commission member for the opposition Francophone Liberals. "This is not what the population expected."

An opinion poll, to be published in Friday's edition of populist paper La Derniere Heure, found almost three-quarters of those polled agreed with the commission's finding. Support was largest in Di Rupo's native Wallonia region.
In a separate poll for the La Meuse-La Lanterne newspapers, also to be published on Friday, only two percent of those asked said a homosexual could not be a government minister.
The commission also approved a draft law simplifying parliamentary procedures for dealing with any allegations against ministers and ex-ministers.

The new law aims would allow the Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, to investigate allegations against ministers without having first to consult parliament. The court still needs parliamentary approval to indict or arrest a minister.

Currently the mere mention of a minister's name in connection with a crime -- concrete evidence is not required -- is enough for a prosecutor to alert the chairman of parliament, who then sets up a special commission of enquiry.
The procedure is highly public and can in itself do such damage to a politician's career that, politically, he is mortally wounded, even if he later turns out to be innocent.

In the Di Rupo case the current climate of scepticism of politics and the justice system had threatened to cost the 45-year-old discreet homosexual his job as the second most senior government politician.

The case had further undermined public confidence in Belgium's establishment already shaken by a child sex and murder scandal that erupted last August. Child rapist Marc Dutroux was arrested in that affair and subsequently the bodies of four young girls weere discovered and two others rescued.
The new draft law, however, means that the Di Rupo could be investigated again if any further allegations emerged.

He has already been cleared of allegations in one case file that he had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 years. He denied the mostly anonymous charges in two other files that were handed to the commission on Monday.
A date for parliament's vote on the law has not been set.
